planting.note: Set out container-grown or grafted trees in spring into deep, moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade while young, and plant a second, genetically distinct cultivar such as Sunflower or Shenandoah within about 30 feet, since Kirsten is self-incompatible like all pawpaws.

directions: Kirsten is a named seedling selection bred by pawpaw enthusiast Tom Mansell at his 'Paw Paw Haven' planting on the bluffs above the Ohio River near Aliquippa, Pennsylvania, from a cross of the older, widely grown Michigan selection 'Taytwo' and the clustered, smooth-fleshed Indiana selection 'Overleese'. It is catalogued alongside the Kentucky State University pawpaw program's compiled regional cultivar table as a named hybrid selection, though unlike the KSU-released cultivars it has not passed through formal multi-state variety trials, so growers should treat it as a collector's selection valued for combining the productivity of its Taytwo parent with the mild, smooth-fleshed dessert quality of Overleese. Trees tolerate deep shade for their first several years but should be given more sun as they mature to maximize fruit set. Because it sits near the northern, cooler end of Pennsylvania pawpaw range, it is a useful genetic option for growers assembling cold-hardy orchard blocks. As with all pawpaws, flowers are pollinated by flies and beetles drawn to their faint carrion scent rather than bees, so hand-pollination with a small brush during the dark maroon spring bloom improves fruit set in home plantings.

planting.note: Set out container-grown or grafted trees in spring into deep, moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade while young, and plant a second, genetically distinct cultivar such as Davis or Sunflower within about 30 feet for cross-pollination.

directions: Ketter traces to a 1916 pawpaw contest sponsored by the American Genetics Association, in which Mrs. Frank Ketter of Ironton, Ohio submitted fruit — shipped packed in excelsior and arriving in perfect condition — that judges rated among the best of roughly 75 trees entered, winning the contest's cash prize. The variety was propagated from her tree, and one of its own seedlings was later named and released as 'Fairchild', giving Ketter a real place in early pawpaw breeding lineage even though, like most of the 1916 contest winners, it never became a widely commercialized nursery item. Fruit is large and yellow with comparatively thick, tough skin that ships and handles better than most old-line selections, ripening early in the pawpaw season with flesh that matures evenly throughout the fruit and a mild but notably rich flavor. Because it predates modern disease-resistance screening, plant it as a genetic-diversity or historical-interest addition alongside a proven modern cultivar rather than relying on it alone for orchard production.
sources: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Research Program — Table 3, Pawpaw Cultivars

common_name: Uncle Tom Pawpaw (Historic First Named Pawpaw Cultivar)

planting.note: Set out container-grown or grafted trees in spring into deep, moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade while young, and plant a second, genetically distinct cultivar within about 30 feet, since Uncle Tom, like all pawpaws, will not set fruit reliably to its own pollen.

directions: Uncle Tom is historically significant as, by most accounts, the first pawpaw selection ever given a cultivar name, predating the organized breeding programs of the 20th century by decades. It was named and propagated by 19th-century Indiana pawpaw and persimmon enthusiast James A. Little of Cartersburg, Indiana, who also established what is considered the first dedicated pawpaw orchard on record. In Little's own descriptions the tree was an extremely heavy bearer, at times fruiting so abundantly that limbs broke under the load, producing large fruit of delicious flavor that ripened around the middle of September and held in good condition on the tree for about a month. Because it predates modern cultivar trials and disease screening, treat Uncle Tom as a living piece of pawpaw breeding history — a genetically distinct, heavy-cropping heirloom worth growing for its story and productivity — and pair it with a proven modern cultivar for the most reliable eating-quality fruit alongside it.
sources: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Research Program — Table 3, Pawpaw Cultivars
Peterson, N. — Pawpaw Variety Development: A History and Future Prospects
North American Pawpaw Growers Association

planting.note: Set out container-grown or grafted trees in spring into deep, moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade while young, and plant a second, genetically distinct cultivar such as Sunflower or NC-1 within about 30 feet for cross-pollination.

directions: Wilson was propagated from a wild seedling tree found growing near Cumberland, Kentucky, and was carried forward into the University of Kentucky and Kentucky State University regional pawpaw variety trials, where it scored well against both older named selections and newer breeding-program releases. The tree itself is notably strong-growing and long-lived, and it produces medium-to-large fruit with good, sweet flavor typical of the better wild Kentucky selections rather than the very largest fruit sizes bred into recent commercial cultivars. Its Appalachian Kentucky origin makes it a useful genetic contributor for growers wanting regionally adapted stock, and it remains available through a handful of specialty native-fruit nurseries. Give young trees consistent moisture and partial shade, moving them into fuller sun as they approach bearing age around year five or six.

common_name: NC-113 Pawpaw (Davis x Overleese Numbered Selection)

planting.note: Set out container-grown or grafted trees in spring into deep, moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade while young, and plant a second, genetically distinct cultivar (not NC-1, its close relative) within about 30 feet for reliable cross-pollination.

directions: NC-113 is a numbered seedling selection from the same Davis x Overleese cross that also produced the well-known commercial cultivar NC-1, but it is a genetically distinct individual selected and documented separately in Kentucky State University's compiled pawpaw cultivar records rather than a synonym for NC-1. Fruit is documented at roughly 10 to 12 ounces, few-seeded, with yellow flesh and yellow skin, consistent with its Davis x Overleese parentage but never commercially released the way NC-1 was. Because it shares grandparentage with NC-1, avoid pairing the two together for pollination — pick a more distantly related cultivar instead. NC-113 is best suited to collectors and gene-bank-style plantings interested in preserving the wider range of seedlings that came out of the historic Davis x Overleese cross rather than home growers who simply want the single most productive tree.
sources: Kentucky State University Pawpaw Research Program — Table 3, Pawpaw Cultivars

planting.note: Set out container-grown or grafted trees in spring into deep, moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade while young, and plant a second, genetically distinct cultivar within about 30 feet for cross-pollination.

directions: Martin originated in Springfield, Ohio and is recorded in Kentucky State University's compiled pawpaw cultivar table as a large-fruited selection with yellow flesh of superior eating quality, noted specifically for withstanding cold well. That documented cold tolerance makes it of particular interest to growers at the northern edge of pawpaw hardiness in zone 4b-5 who have struggled with dieback or crop loss on cultivars bred mainly for the Ohio Valley and points south. As with other historic Ohio-region selections it has not gone through the formal multi-state disease and yield trials that the modern KSU-released cultivars have, so it is best planted as a cold-hardy diversity addition to an orchard rather than the sole named cultivar. Mulch young trees well and provide winter wind protection for the first few years in the coldest end of its range.

planting.note: Set out container-grown or grafted trees in spring into deep, moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade while young, and plant a second, genetically distinct cultivar within about 30 feet for cross-pollination.

directions: Betty Wirt originated in Wirt County, West Virginia and is documented in Kentucky State University's compiled pawpaw cultivar table among the named regional selections gathered from historic pawpaw literature. Fruit can weigh up to a pound at its largest, though typical specimens run closer to 6 ounces, in line with other good wild-origin Appalachian selections of its era. Like most of the West Virginia and Ohio Valley selections cataloged alongside it, it never went through modern multi-state trials or wide commercial release, so treat it as a regionally adapted heirloom valued for genetic diversity and Appalachian provenance in a home orchard rather than a guaranteed top performer. Give young trees consistent moisture and partial shade, moving them into fuller sun as they approach bearing age.
